newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Fur may not fly in EU-Canada row - minister.
newsitem.headline: Fur may not fly in EU-Canada row - minister.

text.p: Canada sees a good chance of resolving a dispute over fur from animals caught in leg-hold traps which has led the European Union to threaten to ban most fur imports, Canada's trade minister said on Wednesday.
Art Eggleton told Reuters after he met with European Union (EU) Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan: "I think we've got a good chance of this agreement being approved."

Brittan "said that he wants to see a successful conclusion of this and that he will be pressing for a successful conclusion, that is acceptance of the agreement that has been initialled with respect to furs," Eggleton said.
Brittan and Eggleton are in Singapore for the World Trade Organisation's ministerial conference.

Earlier this week, EU environment ministers meeting in Brussels threatened to impose an import ban on fur from animals caught in leg-hold traps unless negotiators from Canada, Russia and the United States accepted more humane trapping standards.
Negotiators from Canada, the EU, the United States and Russia have been in talks for months over an agreement on improved trapping standards.

The EU had temporarily suspended a planned ban on imports of fur of species such as muskrats, beavers and sable if they were caught with leg-hold traps, but the ministers instructed the European Commission to take steps to implement the ban by the end of March.
Eggleton said a final EU decision on the matter was several steps away, however, and that Brittan told him no ban would come while the decision was pending.

"It goes to the Commission in one week's time and if it comes through the Commission OK then it will have to go to the council, but it's a question of which council" and when, Eggleton said. But he did not rule out the possibility of individual European countries imposing unilateral bans.
Asked whether, if a Europe-wide ban were imposed, Canada would appeal it through the WTO dispute-resolution mechanism, Eggleton said: "Oh, absolutely."
In Ottawa on Monday, a Canadian official told reporters that if there were such an appeal: "Canada has an extremely strong case and would win."

Canadian officials in Ottawa said the proposed agreement on the fur trade would set improved standards that would be applied not just in Canada, the United States and Russia but also in the EU. They said they were confident a deal would finally be accepted.

But they said if a ban finally took effect, Canada would use the same argument that the EU had used in winning a case against the United States on a U.S. ban on tuna caught with nets that also catch dolphins.
In that case, a WTO panel decided the U.S. restrictions were illegal because an actual tuna did not differ regardless of whether it was caught in an environmentally friendly way.
The EU would have that argument turned against it, the Canadian official said, because the actual fur would not differ if leg-hold traps were banned.
